overview: ’Amuwu is associated with the Chumash community at Mission La Purísima Concepción near present-day Lompoc, California. The detailed evidence here concerns the nineteenth-century mission settlement, rebuilt in 1813 after an earthquake. Its residents maintained relationships, skills and exchange networks while living under coercive colonial institutions.

periods.title: Rebuilding at ’Amuwu
periods.summary: After the 1812 earthquake damaged the earlier mission, construction shifted to the new location. Indigenous workers built housing, workplaces and water infrastructure. This relocation is not a founding date for the Chumash people.

periods.title: Revolt and military recapture
periods.summary: A whipping at Mission Santa Inés helped trigger the Chumash revolt. Rebels occupied La Purísima before soldiers retook it on March 17, 1824. The conflict unfolded under Mexican rule.

periods.title: Secularization and changing livelihoods
periods.summary: Franciscan control ended with secularization, and many Chumash moved into pueblo communities and worked on ranchos. In 1845, Chumash workers Elceario and Pastor Choyama received part of the former mission lands.

periods.title: Investigating the community’s belongings
periods.summary: An archaeological project brought students together with Chumash participants and cultural resource monitor Gina Mosqueda-Lucas. Excavation and community knowledge helped interpret the material traces of Native lives at the mission.

items.text: Excavators found an earthen floor beneath collapsed roof tiles in an adobe building occupied by a Chumash family. A dense deposit behind the building contained discarded material and traces of activity. Studying the room together with its backyard reveals how domestic space was used and maintained.

A larger refuse deposit farther north may mark an area of tule-thatched houses, according to the investigators. Differences in food remains, beads and displayed wealth suggest social distinctions within the community. The house identification and status explanation are interpretations, not a complete reconstruction of every household.

The district’s waterworks connected reservoirs, tile channels, distribution boxes and filtering structures with fields and shared facilities. Supplying water required coordinated construction and maintenance. The historic nomination credits Native craftsmanship; today’s park also includes restored or reconstructed structures that should not be confused with untouched mission-era fabric.

Chumash laborers made bricks, worked wood and built the relocated mission. These were skilled contributions to substantial buildings and working infrastructure. Describing that expertise does not turn the mission labor system into a voluntary building project or attribute the achievement solely to its Franciscan overseers.

sections.title: Food and exchange in the archaeological record

items.text: The 2019 excavations recovered cattle and sheep bones together with remains of local animals and marine fish. California mussels dominated the identified shellfish assemblage. These finds show a diet combining introduced livestock with continuing use of coastal resources, rather than a complete replacement of older foodways.

One floor tile in the Chumash residential building preserved a hoofprint. The study identifies it as an ungulate print, probably from a calf or sheep. It records an animal encountering the tile while the material was impressionable; it does not establish that livestock normally lived inside the room.

Shell beads occurred with Olivella manufacturing debris, evidence that residents made beads locally. Many recovered beads had been drilled with introduced steel needles. The authors connect production with continuing exchange networks. The debris supports manufacture more directly than finished beads alone, which could also have arrived through trade.

A concentration of glass and ceramic vessels was found under a floor in the adobe barracks. Earlier researchers associated the objects with a European resident. Brown and Liguori reexamined the collection and argued that an Indigenous family had occupied the room, challenging identification based simply on imported possessions.

The same study proposes that the household belonged to a Native official or another influential couple known through mission roles such as interpreter, nurse, witness or godparent. It interprets the vessels as a Mexican-period cache. These are argued possibilities, not a securely identified owner’s personal inventory.

Brown’s public archaeology account describes continued manufacture of water-bottle baskets lined with asphaltum, a natural bitumen. It also records ceramic and glass fragments shaped into projectile points. Residents combined established technical knowledge with newly available materials; adoption of imported goods did not require abandoning all older practices.

Chumash collaborators used the Samala-English Dictionary to identify Amuwu as a place name connected with La Purísima. Tribal Historic Preservation Officer Nakia Zavalla emphasized calling archaeological objects belongings. These contributions link language and material evidence with present community relationships, rather than treating the site as an exclusively vanished world.

The 1824 occupation and its military suppression were followed by further institutional change under secularization. The later land grant to Elceario and Pastor Choyama documents Native people acting within the transformed landscape. Neither the end of Franciscan management nor the deterioration of mission buildings meant the disappearance of Chumash people.

ending.text: Mission authority and residence patterns changed through revolt, secularization and movement to ranchos. Chumash descendants continue to interpret this history through language, family accounts and participation in archaeology. The map’s 1500 endpoint does not describe the end of this community, and its early polygon is not established by the later mission evidence.
